findings.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — [P1, confidence 100] `record.match_count += 1` makes a validation predicate mutate telemetry, so the create path's explicit `user.valid?` followed by `user.save` validates twice and records two matches for one signup attempt even when every test passes; the counterargument that callbacks are convenient does not restore one-attempt/one-count semantics, and moving counting to the rejected-request boundary removes this coupling.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — [P1, confidence 100] `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares raw, case-sensitive strings without the canonicalization used elsewhere for email identity, so a blocked address is accepted under different casing and duplicate differently-cased policy rows can represent the same mailbox.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:5 — [P2, confidence 100] `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` leaves `action_type` unconstrained, so any persisted integer outside `actions` silently acquires `do_nothing` behavior and violates the model's two-state policy invariant.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — [P2, confidence 75] `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` materializes server policy decisions as long-lived controller state with no reset or invalidation boundary, so reopening the signup modal continues rejecting addresses based on stale responses; the counterargument that this avoids repeat requests does not justify duplicating mutable policy state, and deleting this cache keeps the server authoritative.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — [confidence 100][severity P1] `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a case-sensitive full-address lookup without normalizing either operand, so a block for `user@example.com` is definitively bypassed by the equivalent address `user@EXAMPLE.COM` even though email domains are case-insensitive.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — [confidence 100][severity P2] `record.match_count += 1` makes validation itself mutate match statistics, so the create flow's explicit `user.valid?` followed by `user.save` validates the same blocked address twice and records two matches for one signup attempt.

spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:17 — [confidence 100][severity P2] `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?).with(record.email).returns(true)` verifies only a stubbed validator call, while no added spec exercises a real blocked row through `User` creation or the controller JSON/rejected-email UI path, leaving the feature's required end-to-end enforcement and propagation entirely unverified.

db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:3 — [P1, confidence 100] Adding `create_table :blocked_emails` to the already-shipped `20130724201552` migration leaves upgraded databases without the table because Rails records the version as applied and never reruns it, so every changed-email validation reaches `BlockedEmail.where` and fails instead of validating; although fresh installs create the table, that does not repair the production upgrade path and this must be a new migration version.

db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:3 — [confidence 100][severity P1] The newly added `create_table :blocked_emails do |t|` is placed inside the pre-existing migration version `20130724201552`, so every upgraded database that already recorded that version skips this code and then `BlockedEmail.where(...)` fails at runtime because the table does not exist; the strongest counterargument is that fresh databases run the migration successfully, but it does not survive because normal upgrades retain `schema_migrations` history and require a new timestamped migration.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — (P2, confidence 100%) `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` mutates match statistics during validation, and `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` before `user.save` revalidates the same user, so every rejected signup is silently counted twice even though the apparent counterargument that validation is read-only is exactly what this new side effect invalidates.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — (P2, confidence 100%) `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write whose concurrent executions overwrite increments, so a spam burst silently undercounts the matches the counter exists to measure; low traffic only makes this work today and does not protect the request path when parallel attempts arrive.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — (P3, confidence 100%) `record.save` has its false return value ignored, so any validation or persistence rejection still returns the configured blocking decision while silently dropping `match_count` and `last_match_at`, producing partial success with no operational signal.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — (P3, confidence 75%) `rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)` retains every distinct server-rejected address without a cap or reset and then linearly scans the list on each validation, so the modal works today for ordinary retries but degrades and preserves stale rejection decisions during a long-lived or automated session despite the counterargument that typical users submit only a few addresses.

app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — P3 confidence 100: `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` expands every failed account-creation response with name and username, creating an unrelated public response-contract change and needless reflection of those fields; although the client needs the submitted email to remember a rejected address, it never consumes name or username, so those additions remain untraceable to blocked-email validation.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — [confidence 100][severity P1] `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs an unnormalized exact lookup, so an attacker bypasses a block for `user@example.com` by registering the same mailbox as `user@EXAMPLE.COM` (email domains are case-insensitive); the strongest counterargument is that exact matching preserves the theoretically case-sensitive local part, but it does not apply because changing only domain casing preserves mailbox identity while defeating enforcement.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — P1 (75% confidence): the new `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` rejection-cache branch has no client or request-contract test, so a key-shape change or stale controller-scoped `rejectedEmails` state can silently leave a rejected address resubmittable or poison a later signup while the Ruby-only suite passes; the branch is short, but it coordinates serialized server data, Ember reactivity, and controller lifecycle that unit coverage elsewhere does not exercise.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the BlockedEmail model only validates presence and uniqueness of email, but does not validate that action_type is constrained to the valid enum values (0 for :block, 1 for :do_nothing). The diff shows the model uses an Enum for actions and the should_block? method checks `record.action_type == actions[:block]`, meaning any invalid integer would fail this check and effectively behave as 'do_nothing'. While the set_defaults callback sets a default, there's no validation preventing invalid values from being persisted. This is a legitimate architectural concern about data integrity, though not strictly a bug since the code would still function (just with unexpected behavior for invalid data).

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that `rejectedEmails` is initialized as controller state with `Em.A([])` and emails are pushed to it when server returns errors (line 274). The diff shows no mechanism to clear this array when the modal is reopened or when the user changes context. This means if an email is rejected once (e.g., due to being blocked), it will remain in the `rejectedEmails` array for the lifetime of the controller, causing the client-side validation to reject that email even if the server-side policy changes. This is a real behavioral issue where stale client state can override current server policy.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff: 1) EmailValidator.validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) which increments match_count and updates last_match_at. 2) The User model has 'validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?' which triggers this validator. 3) In typical Rails create flows, validation runs during both explicit valid? checks and during save. The users_controller.rb shows 'user.save' being called, and if there's an explicit valid? call before save (common pattern), or if validation runs multiple times, the statistics would be incremented multiple times for a single signup attempt. This is a legitimate bug where the side-effect of incrementing statistics in a validation method causes incorrect counting.
